meta.title: When Controls Raise the Cost
meta.subtitle: China’s Responses to U.S. Advanced-Compute Restrictions
meta.question: Since October 2022, which Chinese responses have actually weakened U.S. controls on advanced AI chips, and which have only made Chinese AI development more expensive, slower, or more dependent on outside technology?
meta.currentFinding: One response weakens a narrow control point; none proves system-wide independence.
meta.summary: The public record shows meaningful adaptation, one narrow case of functional substitution, and real enforcement leakage. It does not show that Chinese developers have escaped the cost, scale, or supply-chain consequences of U.S. controls.
meta.conversationSummary: Chinese AI progress is real, but progress and control failure are not synonyms. DeepSeek-V3 shows that efficient model and systems design can stretch a restricted Nvidia H800 fleet. Huawei’s Pangu Ultra shows that thousands of domestic Ascend accelerators can complete a very-large-model training run, weakening the narrow claim that access to top U.S. accelerators is indispensable. CloudMatrix384 shows that system design can recover useful inference performance by pooling many weaker devices. A U.S. prosecution shows that restricted H100 and H200 chips also moved through a diversion network. Each result carries a different implication. The Huawei cases still leave fabrication, high-bandwidth memory, power, networking, and economics unresolved. DeepSeek remained dependent on controlled foreign hardware. Smuggling is an enforcement failure, not technological independence. The strongest current reading is that the controls impose friction and shift costs rather than create an absolute barrier—and that only repeated, independently verified scale can show whether that friction is durable.

responseTypes.label: Domestic substitutes
responseTypes.definition: Chinese-designed accelerators or production inputs replace controlled foreign technology.

responseTypes.label: Compute efficiency
responseTypes.definition: Algorithms and software obtain more useful capability from a fixed hardware budget.

responseTypes.label: Systems engineering
responseTypes.definition: Networks, software, and scale combine weaker devices into a more capable system.

responseTypes.label: Rerouted access
responseTypes.definition: Restricted chips or compute services are reached through intermediaries or offshore infrastructure.

responseTypes.label: Stockpiling & state support
responseTypes.definition: Installed inventories, subsidies, procurement, or tax support absorb or delay the constraint.

classifications.label: Genuine weakening
classifications.definition: The relevant capability is restored at useful scale while dependence falls at the targeted control point.

classifications.label: Adaptation + cost penalty
classifications.definition: The capability is real, but added hardware, energy, time, engineering, or outside dependence remains.

classifications.label: Circumvention, not independence
classifications.definition: Access bypasses enforcement but remains tied to controlled foreign technology and a disruptable route.

classifications.label: Insufficient evidence
classifications.definition: The public record cannot connect the response to restored capability, scale, or a particular rule.

sixQuestions: What AI capability was restored, and on which tasks?
Can it work repeatedly at useful scale?
What extra hardware, electricity, money, engineering, or time does it require?
Does it reduce dependence on technology controlled by the United States or its allies?
Could a realistic enforcement change break the workaround?
Can it support the next generation of development, or only current needs?
sourceHierarchy: Rules, court records, regulatory filings, and official policy documents
Technical disclosures, model cards, repositories, and reproducible benchmarks
Peer-reviewed research and clearly labelled preprints
Independent technical evaluation and specialist analysis
Careful reporting used only where primary evidence is unavailable
limitations: Exact chip inventories, acquisition dates, manufacturing yields, energy use, subsidies, and total engineering costs are usually private.
The Pangu and CloudMatrix performance evidence is vendor-authored and has not been independently reproduced at full scale.
Benchmark gains mix the effects of algorithms, data, hardware, and implementation; they do not isolate the causal effect of export controls.
Enforcement cases reveal detected schemes, not the prevalence of undetected diversion or the capability ultimately produced.
Rules changed repeatedly. Each response must be matched to the rule and license policy in force at that time.
This MVP is selective, not exhaustive. It favors cases with inspectable public evidence and labels gaps instead of estimating hidden quantities.
whatWouldChangeMind: Repeated, independently audited frontier-scale training on domestically fabricated accelerators with disclosed HBM, yield, power, cost, and volume would move the domestic-substitute finding toward broad control failure.
Metered CloudMatrix deployments showing cost and power parity—not only per-TFLOPS efficiency—would weaken the current cost-penalty judgment.
Evidence that diversion or offshore access reliably supplies next-generation compute after realistic customer, ownership, and data-center checks would show a durable enforcement failure.
Audited firm-level data showing no material delay, redesign, inventory drawdown, or cost increase after a matched rule change would challenge the claim that controls still impose friction.
Conversely, documented project delays, unmet accelerator demand, falling training scale, or sustained upstream shortages would strengthen the cost-imposition finding.

timeline.title: Foundational advanced-compute and semiconductor controls
timeline.summary: Created advanced-computing ECCNs, China-wide license requirements, supercomputer end-use controls, foreign-direct-product rules, and specified U.S.-person restrictions.
timeline.caveat: Different provisions took effect on 7, 12, and 21 October; later rules changed thresholds and scope.

timeline.title: Performance-density and anti-circumvention update
timeline.summary: Recalibrated chip thresholds, added a performance-density test, expanded destination and end-user reach, and tightened equipment and U.S.-person controls.
timeline.caveat: The Federal Register publication date is 25 October, despite a conflicting date on one legacy BIS page.

timeline.title: HBM, manufacturing-equipment, software, and entity package
timeline.summary: Added controls on high-bandwidth memory, more semiconductor-manufacturing equipment, ECAD/TCAD software, additional foreign-produced items, and 140 Entity List entries.
timeline.caveat: Limited exceptions and delayed compliance mean this was not a universal HBM or equipment ban.

timeline.title: AI Diffusion Framework issued
timeline.summary: Added worldwide regional-stability licensing for the most advanced chips and controls on certain closed-weight model weights, with country tiers and exceptions.
timeline.caveat: Commerce announced non-enforcement and intended rescission on 13 May 2025 before compliance began; that was not a final legal repeal.

timeline.title: Foundry and packaging due-diligence rule
timeline.summary: Required front-end fabricators and OSATs to investigate designers and customers and created trusted-designer and approved-OSAT pathways.
timeline.caveat: A 2026 amendment extended some designer-status deadlines through 31 December 2026 without removing the core regime.

timeline.title: Validated End-User authorizations revoked for three China fabs
timeline.summary: Removed Intel Dalian, Samsung China Semiconductor, and SK hynix Semiconductor China from the VEU list, requiring individual licenses for covered items.
timeline.caveat: BIS stated it would distinguish existing operations from expansion; TSMC was not named in this rule.

timeline.title: Listed-entity affiliate rule issued, then suspended
timeline.summary: Extended certain end-user restrictions to entities owned 50 percent or more by listed parties and imposed ownership diligence.
timeline.caveat: The automatic affiliates rule was not operative on this project’s 2 September 2026 cutoff date.

timeline.title: Conditional case-by-case review for H200-class exports
timeline.summary: Moved qualifying direct U.S. exports of H200, MI325X, and similar chips to China or Macau from a presumption of denial to conditioned case-by-case review.
timeline.caveat: This was not license-free access or general approval; reexports, transfers, volume, end use, testing, and customer conditions remained restrictive.

cases.title: DeepSeek-V3 on Nvidia H800
cases.finding: Algorithm and systems co-design stretched a restricted H800 fleet, but did not replace the hardware chokepoint.

tests.label: Capability restored
tests.answer: A 671B-parameter mixture-of-experts model delivered strong code, math, science, and chat performance; independent evaluation placed it near models from roughly six months earlier.

tests.label: Repeatable scale
tests.answer: One 2,048-H800 training run is documented. Weights and inference code are public, but the full training stack and dataset are not.

tests.label: Extra resources
tests.answer: The disclosed 2.788 million GPU-hours exclude prior research, ablations, data, staff, acquisition, energy, and failed work. Extensive low-level co-design was required.

tests.label: Outside dependency
tests.answer: Training used Nvidia H800 accelerators and a software/networking stack centered on controlled U.S. technology.

tests.label: Enforcement resilience
tests.answer: Algorithms and weights diffuse readily; installed chips cannot be recalled. Future hardware refresh, HBM, and accelerator replenishment remain enforceable chokepoints.

tests.label: Next generation
tests.answer: The run proves useful 2024-era capability. Later DeepSeek releases do not publicly disclose enough hardware detail to show that the same mechanism scales forward.

uncertainties: Hardware used for later DeepSeek models

cases.title: Pangu Ultra MoE on 6,000 Ascend NPUs
cases.finding: A full large-model training run on Ascend weakens direct accelerator denial, but not upstream controls or the cost-of-scale argument.

tests.label: Capability restored
tests.answer: Huawei reports end-to-end training of a 718B-parameter model, with self-reported results near DeepSeek-R1 on several tasks.

tests.label: Repeatable scale
tests.answer: One 6,000-NPU training run and a 32-card serving recipe are public. The full pretraining pipeline has not been independently reproduced.

tests.label: Extra resources
tests.answer: The run used 6,000 accelerators, about 19 trillion tokens, 30 percent model FLOP utilization, and extensive recomputation, swapping, topology, operator, and simulation work.

tests.label: Outside dependency
tests.answer: Accelerator design and the main software stack are Chinese. Public evidence does not resolve HBM, fabrication equipment, packaging, optics, or the provenance of every die.

tests.label: Enforcement resilience
tests.answer: Domestic accelerators reduce leverage at the finished-chip layer. HBM, EDA, fab tools, foundry services, and packaging remain alternative control points.

tests.label: Next generation
tests.answer: The run shows 2025-scale training is possible; there is no independent evidence of parity with the 2026 frontier or sufficient fleet volume for repeated runs.

uncertainties: Energy, time, yield, and capital cost

cases.title: CloudMatrix384 serving DeepSeek-R1
cases.finding: Pooling Ascend devices restores useful large-model inference, while shifting the constraint into chip count, networking, power, and custom engineering.

tests.label: Capability restored
tests.answer: The vendor-authored evaluation serves a 671B-parameter DeepSeek-R1 model with little reported INT8 accuracy loss across 16 benchmarks.

tests.label: Repeatable scale
tests.answer: A production-grade 384-device architecture and production-representative workloads are described, but no independent fleet-volume audit is public.

tests.label: Extra resources
tests.answer: The complete system uses 384 NPUs, 192 CPUs, a large optical fabric, disaggregated memory, custom collectives, scheduling, quantization, and fault recovery.

tests.label: Outside dependency
tests.answer: The accelerator, CPU, and primary software stack are Chinese; HBM, fab tools, packaging, and high-speed optics remain unresolved.

tests.label: Enforcement resilience
tests.answer: Pooling weakens a per-chip threshold. Aggregate HBM, networking, energy, manufacturing equipment, and production volume remain observable constraints.

tests.label: Next generation
tests.answer: Evidence is strongest for production inference, not frontier pretraining. It does not remove the need for more efficient future devices.

cases.title: Operation Gatekeeper GPU diversion network
cases.finding: A guilty plea and seizures prove material diversion, but not a durable supply route or the AI capability produced by the chips.

tests.label: Capability restored
tests.answer: The chips could support advanced training and inference, but public court and agency materials do not identify a completed model or workload.

tests.label: Repeatable scale
tests.answer: The pleaded conduct covered exported and attempted shipments worth at least $160 million; authorities also seized more than $50 million in technology and cash.

tests.label: Extra resources
tests.answer: The route required straw purchasers, intermediaries, mislabeled hardware, false paperwork, warehouses, logistics companies, and large cross-border payments.

tests.label: Outside dependency
tests.answer: The route depended on Nvidia accelerators and foreign procurement and logistics. It created no domestic technological independence.

tests.label: Enforcement resilience
tests.answer: Customer checks, beneficial-ownership review, shipment inspection, data-center verification, and financial tracing can disrupt this route; this case was disrupted.

tests.label: Next generation
tests.answer: Diversion can provide batches of current chips, but repeated access to each new generation remains exposed to enforcement changes.

uncertainties: Number of GPUs delivered to end users

cases.title: Tax preferences and local compute subsidies
cases.finding: Public policy proves support exists; it does not show which controlled capability a named recipient restored or at what net cost.

tests.label: Capability restored
tests.answer: National tax preferences and local compute vouchers support the sector, but no reviewed award record ties them to a specific restored capability in this MVP.

tests.label: Repeatable scale
tests.answer: Program ceilings are public. Firm-level receipts, additionality, and repeat use are not.

tests.label: Extra resources
tests.answer: Subsidies may transfer cost to the state without removing real hardware, energy, or time requirements.

tests.label: Outside dependency
tests.answer: A tax preference or compute voucher does not disclose the origin of chips, memory, networking, or fabrication inputs.

tests.label: Enforcement resilience
tests.answer: Fiscal support can absorb higher prices but cannot itself replace a denied component or protect a foreign access route.

tests.label: Next generation
tests.answer: The policy horizon extends several years, but future technical outcomes cannot be inferred from budget authority alone.

uncertainties: Capability produced per yuan of support

evidence.claim: DeepSeek reports training a 671B-parameter MoE on 14.8 trillion tokens with 2.788 million H800 GPU-hours.
evidence.counterevidence: The run and benchmarks are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced end to end.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: The public report does not establish acquisition dates, electricity use, or total program cost.

evidence.claim: The widely repeated $5.576 million figure is a rental-equivalent training-compute estimate, not an all-in development cost.
evidence.quotationOrData: Prior research and ablation costs “are not included.”
evidence.counterevidence: The narrow figure remains useful for comparing the disclosed final run if its scope is stated.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: R&D, acquisition, depreciation, staff, data, networking, and failed-run costs are undisclosed.

evidence.claim: An independent evaluation found DeepSeek-V3 broadly comparable to leading models released about six months earlier.
evidence.quotationOrData: “on par with state-of-the-art models from 6 months ago.”
evidence.counterevidence: METR used basic elicitation and warned that looping and other failures might understate or distort capability.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: Benchmark performance is task- and elicitation-dependent and does not establish frontier parity.

evidence.claim: Nvidia identified H800 as a product covered by the October 2023 China licensing restrictions.
evidence.quotationOrData: Restrictions on H800 shipments took effect on 23 October 2023.
evidence.counterevidence: DeepSeek may have acquired its H800 fleet before the restriction took effect; acquisition timing is not public.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: The size and provenance of DeepSeek’s remaining controlled-hardware inventory are unknown.

evidence.claim: The public repository enables inference and inspection of model weights but not reproduction of the full training run.
evidence.quotationOrData: The release includes weights and inference examples for Nvidia, AMD, and Ascend.
evidence.location: Repository README, model downloads and inference sections
evidence.counterevidence: Open weights make broad deployment and independent downstream testing possible.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: Training data, the full HAI-LLM stack, and exact full-run configuration are unavailable.

evidence.claim: Huawei reports completing all training stages for a 718B-parameter MoE on 6,000 Ascend 910B NPUs.
evidence.counterevidence: The run is vendor-reported and has no independent full-training audit or reproduction.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: Run duration, energy, capital cost, fleet availability, and yield are not disclosed.

evidence.claim: The model and execution plan were reshaped around NPU constraints, with cumulative interventions raising reported throughput 58.7 percent.
evidence.quotationOrData: 6,000 NPUs; 30% MFU; hierarchical all-to-all; recomputation and host swapping.
evidence.counterevidence: Thirty percent MFU still implies substantial unused peak compute, and no comparable counterfactual run is public.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: The incremental burden caused specifically by controls cannot be separated from normal large-model engineering.

evidence.claim: The official model repository publishes roughly 1.47 TB of weights and documents a minimum 32-card Ascend serving setup.
evidence.quotationOrData: 62 weight shards; four Atlas 800T A2 nodes; 32 64GB cards.
evidence.location: Model card sections 1, 4.1, and 4.4; file tree
evidence.counterevidence: Serving reproducibility does not reproduce pretraining or validate the disclosed training fleet.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: The complete training corpus, code, and run configuration are not public.

evidence.claim: BIS assessed that listed Ascend 910-series chips likely involved U.S. design technology, software, or equipment subject to export rules.
evidence.quotationOrData: The illustrative list names Ascend 910B and 910C.
evidence.location: Pages 1–2, summary, illustrative list, and applicable regulations
evidence.counterevidence: This is an enforcement assessment, not a bill-of-materials audit of the Pangu fleet or CloudMatrix installation.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: The precise origin and legal status of each chip and upstream component are not public.

evidence.claim: CloudMatrix384 connects 384 Ascend NPUs and 192 Kunpeng CPUs through an all-to-all Unified Bus architecture.
evidence.quotationOrData: 384 NPUs, 192 CPUs, disaggregated prefill, decode, and caching.
evidence.counterevidence: The paper is authored by Huawei and SiliconFlow researchers and is not peer reviewed.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: Public fleet volume and production availability outside the disclosed deployment are unknown.

evidence.claim: The disclosed DeepSeek-R1 test achieved 1,943 decode tokens per second per NPU at 49.4 ms, below one profiled H800 result but above another published H800 baseline.
evidence.quotationOrData: 1,943 tokens/s/NPU at 49.4 ms; reported efficiency 1.29 tokens/s/TFLOPS.
evidence.counterevidence: Batch sizes and implementations differ, and the highest prefill result assumes idealized expert load balancing.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: Like-for-like cost, power, reliability, and hardware-count comparisons are unavailable.

evidence.claim: Tighter latency requirements sharply reduced reported per-NPU throughput, exposing the workload sensitivity of the comparison.
evidence.quotationOrData: Throughput fell from 1,943 to 538 tokens/s/NPU as the target tightened from about 50 ms to 15 ms.
evidence.counterevidence: The system still met the stated tighter latency target and maintained useful throughput.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: Real traffic mixes, uptime, and long-run service cost are not independently reported.

evidence.claim: A specialist estimate argues that matching a GB200 NVL72-class system requires substantially more Ascend devices, optical components, and power.
evidence.quotationOrData: Estimated 4.1 times the system power of a GB200 NVL72.
evidence.counterevidence: The estimate is not metered or audited, and the compared systems differ in chip count and configuration.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: No public independent energy, cooling, or total-cost measurement validates the exact multiplier.

evidence.claim: A company and its owner pleaded guilty in a scheme involving at least $160 million of exported and attempted H100 and H200 shipments.
evidence.quotationOrData: Conduct spanned October 2024 to May 2025; more than $50 million was seized.
evidence.counterevidence: The $160 million figure combines completed and attempted exports; not every person described in the release had been convicted.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: The number of chips delivered, ultimate recipients, and resulting AI tasks are not disclosed.

evidence.claim: The public record describes straw purchasers, third-country customers, relabeling, false paperwork, and warehousing as elements of the diversion route.
evidence.quotationOrData: Labels were removed and replaced with a fictitious company name.
evidence.counterevidence: Several details come from charging documents and remain allegations against defendants who had not pleaded guilty.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: The release does not quantify how common comparable networks are.

evidence.claim: BIS identified concrete checks that could expose transshipment, opaque customers, foreign IaaS access, and implausible data-center capacity.
evidence.quotationOrData: Red flags include freight forwarders, undisclosed end users, foreign IaaS, and infrastructure inconsistent with ordered chips.
evidence.location: Pages 1–5, red flags and due-diligence actions
evidence.counterevidence: Guidance does not establish that every recommended check is implemented or effective in every jurisdiction.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: Detection rates and cross-border enforcement capacity are not public.

evidence.claim: China continued national tax-preference eligibility for integrated-circuit production, design, equipment, materials, packaging, and major projects in 2024.
evidence.quotationOrData: The eligibility notice covers sub-28nm production and multiple upstream inputs and services.
evidence.counterevidence: Eligibility rules do not disclose recipients, award value, additionality, or a capability outcome.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: No firm-level causal link to a reviewed AI-chip workaround is established.

evidence.claim: A 2025 Hangzhou policy authorized annual compute vouchers and large-model training support, but no reviewed award record ties that support to DeepSeek-V3.
evidence.quotationOrData: Annual compute-voucher ceiling: CNY 250 million; qualifying model-training support: up to CNY 50 million.
evidence.location: Measures on compute services and large-model training support
evidence.counterevidence: The policy postdates the DeepSeek-V3 release and does not prove DeepSeek received a grant.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: Recipients, disbursements, hardware origin, and capability produced are not public in the reviewed record.

evidence.claim: GAO reports that BIS used interim-final rules partly to reduce pre-rule stockpiling, but this does not establish the scale of any Chinese inventory response.
evidence.quotationOrData: BIS cited avoiding stockpiling as one reason for immediate enforcement.
evidence.counterevidence: A policy concern is not evidence of actual inventory, intent, ownership, or use by a named Chinese developer.
evidence.remainingUncertainty: Firm-level pre-control and legacy inventories remain largely undisclosed.
